title: Pommes Pont-Neuf
subtitle: Classic thick-cut French fried potatoes
excerpt: Large, thick-cut potato batons (roughly 1 cm by 1 cm and 7 cm long) twice-fried in the classical French manner. The largest and most substantial of the French fried potato cuts, named after the oldest bridge in Paris.
sourceNotes: Pommes Pont-Neuf are documented in Escoffier's Le Guide Culinaire (1903) as the standard thick-cut French fried potato, and in Larousse Gastronomique (1938). The name refers to the Pont-Neuf bridge in Paris, where fried potato vendors traditionally traded. The cut is defined by Escoffier as 1 cm square and 7 cm in length.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The first fry can be done up to 2 hours ahead. Hold the par-fried potatoes at room temperature on kitchen paper, then do the second fry just before serving.

content.text: Pommes Pont-Neuf are the thickest and most substantial of the French fried potato repertoire: roughly the size of a thick British chip, about 1 cm square in cross-section and 7 cm long. Like all proper French fried potatoes, they are cooked twice: first at a low temperature to cook the interior, then at high heat to crisp the outside. They are a bistro staple, the obvious companion to steak, duck confit, and grilled lamb.

items.prepNote: floury variety, peeled and cut into 1 cm by 1 cm by 7 cm batons

content.text: Rinse the potato batons in cold water until the water runs clear. Dry very thoroughly with a clean cloth or kitchen paper.

Heat the oil to 140°C in a large, deep, heavy pan. Lower the potato batons in batches and cook for 8 to 10 minutes until cooked through but with almost no colour. Lift out with a slotted spoon, drain on kitchen paper, and cool to room temperature. The interior must be fully cooked at this stage.

Heat the oil to 190°C. Lower the par-fried batons back in, in batches, and cook for 4 to 5 minutes until deep golden and crisp. The thick cut needs longer at high heat than thinner chips. Drain on fresh kitchen paper and season immediately with sea salt flakes.
Serve immediately. These hold their heat well because of the thick cut, but they will lose their crispness as they cool.

items.symptom: Potatoes are soft inside after the second fry
items.cause: First fry was too short, or temperature too high to cook the interior through
items.fix: The first fry at 140°C must cook them all the way through. Test one before lifting the batch out.

items.symptom: Colour is pale despite long second fry
items.cause: Oil temperature dropped too far with a large batch
items.fix: Fry in smaller batches to keep the oil at 190°C.

content.text: The Pont-Neuf cut is named after the bridge in Paris where fried potato sellers were a fixture of street life from the eighteenth century onwards. It is the standard chip cut of the French bistro: thick enough to have a fluffy interior alongside a crisp crust, and substantial enough to anchor a plate of steak or duck. In French cooking the specific cut has a name and a set of dimensions; you would not serve allumettes alongside a confit de canard, nor would you serve Pont-Neuf with a delicate sole meunière. The cut matches the dish.
